games.intro: Play and learn: {n} games for maths, physics, chemistry, biology and more. The difficulty adapts to you.
games.search: Search for a game or topic
games.e.meteor.how: The meteors carry answers. Tap the meteor with the correct answer before it hits the shield. Keys: 1–4 or ← → and space.
games.e.balloons.how: Pop the balloon with the correct answer before time runs out. A wrong balloon costs a life. Keys: ← → and space.
games.e.runner.how: Tap a lane or swipe left and right (keys ← →) to run through the gate with the correct answer.
games.e.sorter.how: Is the statement on the crate true? Tap ✓ or ✗ (keys → and ←) before the crate leaves the belt.
games.e.maze.how: Guide Piko to the right answer. Bugs send you back to the start. Arrows or swipe.
games.e.castle.how: Tap the ledge with the right answer and Arin jumps to it. Keys 1–3.
games.e.snake.how: Steer the snake to the right answer. Arrows or swipe.
games.e.frog.how: Tap the lily pad with the right answer. Keys 1–3.
games.e.moles.how: Whack the mole with the right answer. Keys 1–9.
games.e.heli.how: Fly through the gap with the right answer. Drag with your finger or keys 1–3.
games.e.bricks.how: Move the paddle and hit the brick with the right answer. Tap to launch.
games.e.invaders.how: Shoot the alien with the right answer. Tap, or arrows and Space. Keys 1–4.
games.e.lander.how: Land on the pad with the right answer. Tap a pad or hold your finger where you want to go. Keys 1–3.
games.e.bubbles.how: Aim and shoot a bubble at the right answer. Keys 1–4.
games.e.cannon.how: Drag to set direction and power, release to fire. Knock down the tower with the right answer. Keys 1–3.
games.e.crane.how: Tap to drop the block with the right answer onto the tower. A wrong block knocks the top off.
games.e.marble.how: Tilt the phone to roll the marble into the hole with the right answer, or hold your finger where it should roll. Arrow keys.
games.e.jumper.how: Tilt the phone so Pip lands on the platform with the right answer, or tap where he should go. Keys 1–3.
games.e.orb.how: Shake the phone or tap the arrows button for the next answer. At the right one, tap the orb or ✓.

greek.title: Greek mathematicians
greek.f1: Around 300 BC in Alexandria, Euclid wrote the Elements, 13 books on geometry and numbers. People learned from them for more than 2,000 years, and this app is named after him (Evklid is Slovenian for Euclid).
greek.f2: In the Elements, Euclid proved that there are infinitely many primes: the product of any primes plus 1 always has a prime factor that is not among them.
greek.f3: Euclid's algorithm from the Elements finds the greatest common divisor of two numbers. Today we write it as repeated division with remainder: gcd(48, 18) = gcd(18, 12) = gcd(12, 6) = 6.
greek.f4: According to a story told by Proclus, King Ptolemy I asked Euclid whether there was a shorter way to geometry than the Elements. Euclid is said to have replied: “There is no royal road to geometry.”
greek.f5: The Pythagorean theorem a² + b² = c² is named after Pythagoras (6th century BC), although the Babylonians knew triples such as 3, 4, 5 more than a thousand years earlier.
greek.f6: Thales of Miletus (around 600 BC) is considered one of the first to prove statements in geometry. Thales's theorem is named after him: an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.
greek.f7: Archimedes of Syracuse (3rd century BC) used polygons with 96 sides to show that π lies between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7. Legend has it that he shouted “Eureka!” (I have found it!) in the bath when he worked out how to test the king's gold crown.
greek.f8: Eratosthenes of Cyrene (3rd century BC) used shadows at the summer solstice in Syene (today's Aswan) and Alexandria to estimate the Earth's circumference surprisingly well. The sieve of Eratosthenes for finding primes is also named after him.
greek.f9: Hypatia of Alexandria (died AD 415) was a mathematician, astronomer and philosopher. She is considered the first woman mathematician about whom we know anything reliable; according to the sources, she wrote commentaries on works by Diophantus and Apollonius.
greek.f10: In his Conics (around 200 BC), Apollonius of Perga gave the curves obtained by cutting a cone the names we still use today: ellipse, parabola and hyperbola.
greek.f11: Diophantus of Alexandria (probably 3rd century AD) solved equations in his Arithmetica and was among the first to use an abbreviation for the unknown. Equations whose integer solutions we look for are called Diophantine today.
era.renesansa.title: Renaissance mathematicians
era.renesansa.f1: As early as 1202, Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci, introduced Europeans to Hindu-Arabic numerals and place-value notation in his book Liber Abaci; he had learned them in North Africa. The book also contains the rabbit problem, which gives the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 …: each term is the sum of the two before it.
era.renesansa.f2: In 1494, in his Summa de arithmetica, Luca Pacioli was the first to print a description of double-entry bookkeeping, which Venetian merchants already used. His book On the Divine Proportion (1509), about the golden ratio, was illustrated by Leonardo da Vinci.
era.renesansa.f3: Around 1490 Leonardo da Vinci drew the Vitruvian Man: a male figure whose outstretched arms and legs fit both a circle and a square. The drawing follows the proportions of the human body described by the Roman architect Vitruvius in the 1st century BC.
era.renesansa.f4: In 1539 Niccolò Tartaglia confided to Gerolamo Cardano, in verse, how to solve cubic equations, and Cardano promised not to publish the method. In 1545 he published it anyway in his book Ars Magna (crediting Tartaglia and del Ferro, who had solved the equation earlier), which started a famous quarrel.
era.renesansa.f5: In 1591 François Viète began using letters in equations not only for unknowns (vowels) but also for known quantities (consonants). This lets one formula describe all equations of the same kind, the foundation of today's algebra.
era.renesansa.f6: In 1609, in his New Astronomy, Johannes Kepler showed that Mars moves around the Sun on an ellipse, with the Sun at one of its foci. The ellipse had been described more than 1800 years earlier by Apollonius of Perga.
era.bagdad.title: Mathematicians of the Islamic Golden Age
era.bagdad.f1: Around 820, in Baghdad's House of Wisdom, al-Khwarizmi wrote a book on solving equations by "completion and balancing". The word algebra comes from al-jabr in its title, and the word algorithm from the Latin form of his name (Algoritmi).
era.bagdad.f2: Omar Khayyam (1048–1131) solved cubic equations geometrically, using intersections of conic sections such as a circle and a parabola. He also led the astronomers who prepared a calendar more accurate than the Julian one. He is also known as a poet of quatrains.
era.bagdad.f3: Al-Biruni (973 – c. 1050) measured from a hilltop near Nandana, in today's Pakistan, how far the horizon dips below the horizontal, and from the height of the hill calculated the Earth's radius. His value was close to today's (about 6371 km).
era.bagdad.f4: Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen, c. 965 – c. 1040) showed in his Book of Optics that we see because light travels from objects into the eye, not the other way round, as some Greek scholars had thought. He tested his claims by experiment, so he is counted among the founders of the scientific method.
era.bagdad.f5: Around 1424 in Samarkand, Jamshid al-Kashi calculated π correct to 16 decimal places: 3.1415926535897932. Nobody calculated it more accurately for more than 170 years.
era.bagdad.f6: Thabit ibn Qurra (died 901) found a rule for amicable numbers: pairs in which the sum of the proper divisors of each number equals the other. The smallest such pair is 220 and 284. He also improved the Arabic translation of Euclid's Elements.
era.indija.title: Indian mathematicians
era.indija.f1: In 628, in his Brahmasphutasiddhanta, Brahmagupta wrote down rules for calculating with zero and with negative numbers, which he called "debts" (positive ones were "fortunes"). One rule says that the product of two debts is a fortune: (−2) · (−3) = 6.
era.indija.f2: In AD 499, in his Aryabhatiya, Aryabhata wrote that a circle with a diameter of 20,000 has a circumference of about 62,832, so π ≈ 3.1416. His methods for square and cube roots already rely on decimal place-value notation.
era.indija.f3: The decimal place-value system with zero that we use today developed in India. It reached Europe through Arab scholars such as al-Khwarizmi and through Fibonacci's book Liber Abaci (1202). That is why we call the digits 0–9 Arabic, although they come from India.
era.indija.f4: Bhaskara II (1114–1185) wrote the textbook Lilavati, whose problems are written in verse and often addressed to a girl named Lilavati; according to tradition she was his daughter. In India people learned arithmetic from this book for centuries.
era.indija.f5: Madhava of Sangamagrama (c. 1340 – c. 1425) expressed π as an infinite series: π/4 = 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − 1/7 + … We know his work from the writings of the Kerala school; in Europe Gregory and Leibniz rediscovered the series about 270 years later.
era.indija.f6: Srinivasa Ramanujan (1887–1920) was largely self-taught and left almost 4000 theorems and formulas. When Hardy remarked that the number of his taxi, 1729, seemed dull, Ramanujan, as Hardy told it, replied that it was very interesting: it is the smallest number that is a sum of two cubes in two ways, 1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³.

scan.askStepText: I'm solving {problem}. I don't understand step {n}: “{title}” ({tex}). Can you explain it another way?
scan.askAllText: Help me understand the problem {problem}. The solution is {answer}. Explain the method to me step by step.
scan.solvingAi: This problem is harder. Evklid AI is solving and checking it …
scan.noSolve: I can't solve this problem step by step yet. Ask the tutor.
scan.aiFail: Solving didn't work. Try again or ask the tutor.
scan.a.all: Every real number is a solution.
scan.a.noReal: The equation has no real solutions.
scan.a.sysMany: The system has infinitely many solutions.
scan.s.clearFrac: Clear the fractions: multiply both sides by {n}.
scan.w.clearFrac: {n} is the least common multiple of the denominators. We multiply every term on both sides by it, so the denominators cancel. The equation still has the same solutions.
scan.s.clearDec: Clear the decimals: multiply both sides by {n}.
scan.w.clearDec: We multiply every term on both sides by {n} to get whole numbers. Whole numbers are easier to work with, and the solutions stay the same.
scan.w.dist: Multiply the number in front of the bracket by each term inside it: a(b + c) = ab + ac.
scan.w.distNeg: Multiply the number in front of the bracket by each term inside it. If there is a minus in front of the bracket, every term inside changes its sign.
scan.w.foil: Multiply each term of the first bracket by each term of the second: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd.
scan.w.sqPlus: Square of a sum: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b².
scan.w.sqMinus: Square of a difference: (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².
scan.w.diffSq: Difference of squares: (a − b)(a + b) = a² − b².
scan.w.power: Write the power of the bracket as a product of equal brackets and multiply them out.
scan.w.collect: Like terms have the same variables with the same exponents (e.g. 3x and −5x). Add their coefficients, and add the numbers without variables separately.
scan.s.move: Move the terms with {v} to the left side and the numbers to the right.
scan.w.move: We add or subtract the same term on both sides. That's why it looks as if the term jumped to the other side and changed its sign.
scan.w.divide: To get {v} on its own, divide both sides by its coefficient.
scan.s.divideFlip: Divide both sides by {a}. Since this number is negative, the inequality sign flips.
scan.w.flip: When you multiply or divide an inequality by a negative number, the inequality sign flips (e.g. 2 < 3, but −2 > −3).
scan.s.allX: The equation holds for every value of {v}.
scan.w.allX: The variable {v} has disappeared and what's left is a true statement. So every real number is a solution.
scan.w.noX: The variable {v} has disappeared and what's left is a false statement. So no number solves the equation.
scan.s.allXIneq: The inequality holds for every value of {v}.
scan.s.check: Check: substitute the solution into the original problem.
scan.w.check: The left side ({l}) and the right side ({r}) are equal, so the solution is correct. Do the check yourself too when you solve in your notebook.
scan.w.checkSys: Substitute the solution into both original equations. Both hold, so the solution is correct.
scan.s.interval: Write the solution in interval notation.
scan.w.interval: A round bracket means the endpoint is not a solution (< or >), a square bracket means it is (≤ or ≥). Next to ∞ the bracket is always round.
scan.w.subAll: A double inequality holds when both inequalities hold. We subtract the same number from all three parts at once.
scan.s.standard: Move all terms to the left side.
scan.w.standard: We solve a quadratic equation in standard form ax² + bx + c = 0, with 0 on the right side.
scan.w.standardN: We solve a higher-degree equation with 0 on the right side: then we look for the zeros of the polynomial on the left.
scan.w.negate: This makes the coefficient of the highest power positive, which makes the working easier. The solutions don't change.
scan.s.negateFlip: Multiply the inequality by −1, so the inequality sign flips.
scan.w.reduce: All the coefficients are divisible by the same number. Smaller numbers are easier to work with.
scan.s.coeffs: Read off the coefficients a, b and c.
scan.w.coeffs: In the standard form ax² + bx + c = 0, a is the coefficient of x², b the coefficient of x and c the constant term. Watch the signs.
scan.w.disc: The discriminant tells you how many solutions the equation has: D > 0 two, D = 0 one, D < 0 no real ones.
scan.w.formula: The formula works for every quadratic equation. The ± sign means we get two solutions: once we add, once we subtract.
scan.s.formulaOne: D = 0, so the equation has one (double) solution.
scan.w.formulaOne: When D = 0, √D = 0 and both solutions from the formula are the same.
scan.s.noReal: D < 0, so the equation has no real solutions.
scan.w.noReal: The square root of a negative number is not a real number. The parabola doesn't cross the x-axis.
scan.s.complex: The two solutions in the complex numbers.
scan.w.complex: Write √D using the imaginary unit i, where i² = −1.
scan.w.factorOut: All the terms contain the same factor, so we take it out in front of a bracket.
scan.s.zeroProduct: A product equals 0 when at least one factor equals 0.
scan.w.zeroProduct: If a · b = 0, then a = 0 or b = 0. Set each factor equal to 0 separately.
scan.w.isolateSq: The equation has no linear term (b = 0), so we express x² and take the square root.
scan.s.noRealSq: A square can't be negative, so the equation has no real solutions.
scan.w.noRealSq: The square of every real number is greater than or equal to 0.
scan.s.root: Take the square root of both sides.
scan.w.root: A square equals a given number for two opposite values, so we write ±.
scan.s.vieta: Find two numbers whose product is {p} and whose sum is {s}: they are {m} and {n}.
scan.w.vieta: Vieta's formulas: x² + bx + c = (x + m)(x + n) when m · n = c and m + n = b.
scan.w.vietaTrinomial: Factor the trinomial x² + bx + c as (x + m)(x + n), where m · n = c and m + n = b.
scan.s.acMethod: Find the solutions using Vieta's formulas.
scan.w.vietaA: For ax² + bx + c = 0: x₁ + x₂ = −b/a and x₁ · x₂ = c/a.
scan.s.factored: Write the equation as a product.
scan.w.factored: Check the factorisation by multiplying the brackets back out.
scan.w.divideA: To complete the square, the coefficient of x² should be 1.
scan.s.complete: Complete the square (half of the coefficient of x is {h}).
scan.w.complete: From x² and the x term we build the square of a binomial. Since the square adds {h}², we subtract it straight away.
scan.s.isolateSquare: Isolate the square on the left side.
scan.w.isolateSquare: Move the numbers to the right side and add them up.
scan.s.horner: Guess the zero {r} and divide the polynomial using Horner's method.
scan.w.horner: Rational zeros are among the fractions p/q, where p divides the constant term and q divides the leading coefficient. Since p({r}) = 0, the polynomial is divisible by (x − {r}).
scan.w.solveQuadratic: What's left after dividing is a quadratic polynomial; its zeros are the remaining solutions.
scan.w.zeros: At the zeros the expression equals 0, and between the zeros it keeps its sign.
scan.s.parabolaAbove: The parabola opens upwards; we take the parts where it is above the x-axis.
scan.s.parabolaBelow: The parabola opens upwards; we take the part where it is below the x-axis.
scan.w.parabola: Since a > 0, the parabola is below the x-axis between the zeros and above it outside the zeros.
scan.w.parabolaNoZero: The parabola doesn't cross the x-axis and opens upwards, so it is always above the x-axis.
scan.s.sysNormal: Rearrange both equations into the form a{x} + b{y} = c.
scan.w.sysNormal: Move the unknowns to the left, the numbers to the right, and clear any fractions. This makes the system easier to solve.
scan.w.express: Choose the unknown that is easiest to express (preferably one with coefficient 1 or −1).
scan.s.substitute: Substitute the expression for {v} into equation {n}.
scan.w.substitute: Instead of {v}, write the expression in brackets. You get an equation with one unknown.
scan.w.backSub: Substitute the value you found into the equation where the calculation is easiest.
scan.s.elimMul: Multiply the equations so that the coefficients of {v} are opposite numbers.
scan.w.elimMul: When we add the equations, the opposite coefficients cancel out and {v} disappears.
scan.w.elimAdd: Add the left sides together and the right sides together. You're left with an equation with one unknown.
scan.s.det: Calculate the determinant D of the system.
scan.w.det: A 2 × 2 determinant is the product on the main diagonal minus the product on the other diagonal. If D ≠ 0, the system has exactly one solution.
scan.w.detXY: For D{x}, replace the column of {x} coefficients with the column of right-hand sides; for D{y}, replace the {y} column.
scan.s.cramer: Get the solution with Cramer's rule.
scan.w.cramer: Each unknown is the quotient of its own determinant and the determinant of the system.
scan.w.sysNone: The lines are parallel and don't intersect, so there is no common point.
scan.s.sysDependent: The system has infinitely many solutions.
scan.w.sysDependent: Both equations describe the same line, so every point on it is a solution.
scan.w.paren: The order: brackets first, then powers, then multiplication and division, and finally addition and subtraction.
scan.w.pow: Powers come before multiplication and division.
scan.w.mul: Multiplication and division come before addition and subtraction.
scan.w.div: Division comes before addition and subtraction.
scan.s.muldiv: Multiply and divide from left to right.
scan.w.muldiv: Multiplication and division have equal priority, so we work from left to right.
scan.s.addsub: Add and subtract from left to right.
scan.w.addsub: Addition and subtraction have equal priority, so we work from left to right.
scan.w.common: Rewrite the fractions with the common denominator {d}, then add the numerators.
scan.w.mulFrac: To multiply fractions, multiply the numerators together and the denominators together. Cancel first if you can.
scan.w.divFrac: To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal.
scan.w.divToFrac: If the quotient isn't a whole number, write it as a fraction in lowest terms.
scan.w.negPow: A negative exponent means the reciprocal: a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.
scan.w.commonFactor: Find the greatest common divisor of the coefficients and the lowest power of each variable that appears in every term.
scan.s.cantFactor: The expression can't be factored into simpler factors with rational coefficients.
scan.w.cantFactor: There is no common factor, it doesn't match any formula, and it has no rational zeros.
scan.w.diffSquares: A difference of squares is the product of the difference and the sum of the bases.
scan.s.trinomial: Factor the trinomial using its zeros.
scan.w.trinomial: If x₁ and x₂ are the zeros, then ax² + bx + c = a(x − x₁)(x − x₂).
scan.w.dSum: The derivative of a sum (difference) is the sum (difference) of the derivatives.
scan.s.dConst: The derivative of a constant is 0.
scan.w.dConst: A constant doesn't change, so its derivative is 0.
scan.s.dPower: Differentiate the power: the exponent {n} moves to the front and the exponent decreases by 1.
scan.w.dPower: The power rule works for every exponent, including negative and fractional ones.
scan.s.dConstPower: The coefficient stays, and we differentiate the power: the exponent {n} moves to the front and the exponent decreases by 1.
scan.w.dConstPower: A constant that multiplies the function is copied; we differentiate only the function.
scan.s.dConstMul: The constant stays; differentiate the function.
scan.w.dConstMul: A constant that multiplies or divides the function is copied; we differentiate only the function.
scan.w.dProduct: Product rule: differentiate the first factor and copy the second, then copy the first and differentiate the second, and add.
scan.w.dQuotient: Quotient rule: (derivative of the numerator · denominator − numerator · derivative of the denominator) divided by the square of the denominator.
scan.s.dChain: Use the chain rule (derivative of a composite function).
scan.w.dChain: First differentiate the outer function and copy the inner one, then multiply by the derivative of the inner function.
scan.s.dTable: Read the derivative from the table of derivatives.
scan.w.dTable: We learn the derivatives of the basic functions by heart or look them up in a table.
scan.w.dExp: The derivative of eˣ is eˣ. If the exponent is an expression, differentiate it too and multiply (chain rule).
scan.w.dGeneric: Use the rules for the derivative of a sum, a product, a quotient and a composite function.
scan.s.dCombine: Add up the derivatives of the terms.
scan.w.dCombine: Combine the derivatives of the individual terms and write the result as simply as possible.
scan.desk: Choose a picture of the problem, paste a screenshot (Ctrl + V) or turn on the camera.
scan.s.moveRight: Move the terms with {v} to the right side and the numbers to the left.
scan.s.standardRight: Move all terms to the right side and swap the sides.
scan.s.domain: A denominator must not be 0, so {v} must not be:
scan.w.domain: We can't divide by 0. If we end up with one of these values, it is not a solution.
scan.s.mulLcd: Multiply both sides by the common denominator {d}.
scan.w.mulLcd: The common denominator is the product of all the different factors in the denominators. When we multiply every term by it, the fractions cancel.
scan.s.reject: {v} = {r} is not a solution, because a denominator would be 0.
scan.w.reject: A value that would make us divide by 0 is not in the domain, so we discard it.
scan.s.numeric: There are no rational roots, so we find the roots numerically (by bisection).
scan.w.numeric: Bisection: we keep halving an interval on which the polynomial changes sign until it is small enough. You can also see the roots on the graph.
